main.text: That the bird דרור deror is not the swallow, as is held, but a kind of wild dove, namely the turtledove or the wood pigeon.

Among the birds there is one which the Hebrews call דרור deror, that is, freedom, or the free one; מפני שחרה בבית כבשרה, because it moves about as freely in the house as in the field. So R. Ishmael holds in the Talmudic tractate Betsa, ch. 3, p. 24a. Hence the later Hebrews, and the recent lexicographers and Bible translators who have followed them, hold with complete agreement that דרור deror is the swallow, because two species of swallows are said to exist,
of which one seeks the woods, the other goes beneath roofs. — — — — ^{a)}

But this reasoning is not sufficient, since there are other birds too, some domestic, some wild. Among these doves hold first place: one kind of them is κατοικίδιον [katoikidion], domestic, the other νομαδικὸν [nomadikon], roaming and feeding in the fields, as is found in Galen, book 10 De Simplic. Varro makes the same distinction in Rustic. book 3, ch. 7, yet in such a way that he says both kinds live in buildings; but the wild kind in the uppermost part of towers, from which it flies out into the fields and returns, whereas the other, tamer kind, content with household food, usually feeds within the threshold of the door. I think that the name דרור deror signifies both this wild kind of dove and whatever species of doves the Greeks list among the wild ones, but above all φάτταν [phattan], the wood pigeon, and τρυγόνα [trygona], the turtledove. I am moved to this, first, by the authority of the ancient translators, who explain דרור as either the turtledove or the wood pigeon. Thus in Ps. LXXXIV, 4 דרור is rendered turtledove in the Greek version, and in the Vulgate, the Chaldee, the Syriac, and both Arabic versions, and in the paraphrase of Apollinaris. But the Ethiopic has መዐንቅ፡, that is, the collared one: an epithet by which, as everyone knows, the wood pigeon is distinguished, on account of the collar it has around its neck. Martial in the Xenia:
The collared wood pigeons slow and dull the loins.
Abdorrachman, son of Abubecr, in his poem On the Divorce of Atica, once his dearest wife,

ما ناح قمري الحمام المطوق [mā nāḥa qumrī al-ḥamām al-muṭawwaq] [col. 52] [II, 591] How the wood pigeon, the ring-necked dove, laments. Alkazuinius [=al-Qazwīnī, ʿAjāʾib al-makhlūqāt]: ان بيض القماري يجعل تحت الفواخت وبيض الفواخت يجعل تحت القماري كلاهما ينغقان قماري كافورية مطوقة [inna bayḍ al-qamārī yujʿal taḥt al-fawākhit wa-bayḍ al-fawākhit yujʿal taḥt al-qamārī kilāhumā yanghaqān qamārī kāfūriyya muṭawwaqa] Whether the eggs of the wood pigeon are placed under the phabe, or the eggs of the phabe under the wood pigeon, nothing will be hatched from them but camphor-coloured, ring-necked wood pigeons. The other derivation is taken from the Arabic language, in which الحر [al-ḥurr] alhorro is the young of a dove or of a turtledove, and ساق حر [sāq ḥurr] sako horrin is the wood pigeon. Alcamus [=al-Qāmūs al-muḥīṭ, the Arabic dictionary of al-Fīrūzābādī, which Bochart cites like an author]: الحر فرخ الحمامة [al-ḥurr farkh al-ḥamāma] Alhorro, the young of a dove; Giggeius [=Antonio Giggei, Thesaurus linguae Arabicae (Milan 1632)] adds, or of a turtledove. ساق حر ذكر القماري [sāq ḥurr dhakar al-qamārī] Sako horrin, the male of the wood pigeons. And elsewhere: الورشان طاير وهو ساق حر لحمه اخف من الحمام [al-warashān ṭāyir wa-huwa sāq ḥurr laḥmuhu akhaff min al-ḥamām] Alvvarsen, a bird, namely sako horrin, whose flesh is lighter than that of the dove. The Arabs say it is so called from its call. Ibn Sida: سمي القماري ساق حر لصوته فانه يقول ساق حر ساق حر [summiya al-qamārī sāq ḥurr li-ṣawtihi fa-innahu yaqūl sāq ḥurr sāq ḥurr] The wood pigeon is called sako horrin on account of its call, because it says Sako horrin, Sako horrin. In the same way another species of wood pigeon, قطا [qaṭā] kata or katta, is also thought to be named from its call. Damir [=al-Damīrī, Ḥayāt al-ḥayawān]: سميت بحكاية صوته [summiyat bi-ḥikāyat ṣawtihi] It has its name from the likeness of its call. For, they say, when it comes to its young, bringing water in its crop, صاحت قطا قطا [ṣāḥat qaṭā qaṭā] it cries Katta, Katta. But this is pure invention. For قطا [qaṭā] katta is bent from the Greek name of the wood pigeon, φάττα [phatta]. The Arabs often change Greek φ and π into Kaph, because among them ف Phe and ق Kaph have the same shape and differ only in the dots, Phe having a single one and Kaph a double. Accordingly in Avicenna [=Ibn Sīnā, al-Qānūn fī l-ṭibb (the Canon)] قوقي [qūqī] kauke are seals. In the Arabic Dioscorides قوطوما [qūṭūmā] is φύτευμα [phyteuma], قوقي [qūqī] keuke is πεύκη [peukē], قرقسيون [qarqasiyūn] karkesion is καρπήσιον [karpēsion], قوقس البحر [qūqas al-baḥr] kukos albahri is φύκος θαλάσσιον [phykos thalassion]. That this is not a slip of the copyists but of the authors is clear from the fact that these words are arranged in alphabetical order and are listed under the letter Kaph. Thus, then, قطا [qaṭā] Kata or katta is φάττα [phatta], that is, the wood pigeon, and it is not named from its call, as the Arabs imagine. The same judgement applies to ساق حر [sāq ḥurr] sako horrin. For ساق [sāq] sako by itself is the male of the dove. And ساق حر [sāq ḥurr] sako horrin is the male of the dove of liberty, or of the free dove, that is, of the wood pigeon, or also of the turtledove, as some hold. For like the Hebrew דרור deror, so the Arabic حر [ḥurr] horro means free. And the root حر [ḥarra], in Syriac and Chaldee חרר harar, means to be free and to grant freedom. Therefore, whenever דרור is taken in the sacred text for liberty, the Chaldee [col. 53] [II, 592] translators have חירות in its place, and the Arabic ones حرية [ḥurriyya]. Nor indeed is it obscure why among the Orientals wild and field doves are named from liberty. For Basil too, in Epistle 175 to Julitta, calls a flock of such doves αὐτόνομον ἀγέλην [autonomon agelēn], a free flock, living by its own laws. For in Greek αὐτόνομος [autonomos] is the same as ἐλεύθερος [eleutheros]. Hence Thucydides in book 2 calls the same peoples indiscriminately αὐτονόμους [autonomous] and ἐλευθέρους [eleutherous]. And in Plutarch, in the dialogue On the Daemon of Socrates, Epaminondas declares himself a citizen ἐλευθέρας καὶ αὐτονόμου πόλεως [eleutheras kai autonomou poleōs]. And Demosthenes, in the First Philippic, says of the peoples who were of Philip's party: αὐτονομούμενα καὶ ἐλεύθερα (ἔθνη) ὑπῆρχε [autonomoumena kai eleuthera (ethnē) hypērche]. Accordingly Isocrates opposes αὐτονομίαν [autonomian] to servitude, saying that under Evagoras the Greeks had ἀντὶ δουλείας αὐτονομίαν [anti douleias autonomian]. Therefore, following Basil, you would rightly render the Hebrew דרור deror as αὐτόνομον περιστεράν [autonomon peristeran].

In the two passages of Scripture in which דרור deror occurs for a bird, there is nothing that conflicts in the least with this interpretation. In Prov 26:2 the דרור seems to be commended for the swiftness of its flight, in which, as we have shown in its place ^{R1}, the dove can compete with any bird whatever. And in Ps 84:4 the Psalmist groans, comparing his lot with the meanest birds, namely the sparrow and the דרור deror, that is, the field dove, to which not only free access to the altar of God was granted, but also to nest and hatch their young there, while he himself was a wanderer, an exile, and far from the sacred house. In the name of the altar there must be a figure of speech. For amid so great a throng of men and sacrifices, staying on the altar itself would not have been safe for birds. Therefore altar is put for the tabernacle, or for the temple: for the tabernacle if David speaks in this Psalm; for the temple if someone else after David ^{R2}. For the Hebrews are in doubt, as one may learn from Kimchi [=David Kimḥi (Radak), Sefer ha-Shorashim]. However that may be, both the tabernacle [II, 593] and the temple ^{b)} rested on great beams of cedar and of ἀρκευθίναις [arkeuthinais], in which kind of cedar the wood pigeon likes to nest, as these lines of Theocritus, Idyll 5, teach.

Κἠγὼ μὲν δώσω τᾷ παρθένῳ αὐτίκα φάσσαν, Ἐκ τᾶς ἀρκεύθῳ καθελὼν, τηνεὶ γὰρ ἐφείσδει. [Kēgō men dōsō tai parthenōi autika phassan, Ek tas arkeuthō kathelōn, tēnei gar epheisdei.] But you, my maiden, happy one, shall be given a wood pigeon, whose nest lies hidden in the lofty timber of a juniper.

But Albertus and Turner also assert that the livia dove nests in temples. And it is known from Herodotus ^{c)} what happened to Aristodicus when ἐξαῖρε τοὺς στρουθοὺς, καὶ ἄλλα ὅσα ἦν νενοσσευμένα ὀρνίθων γένεα ἐν τῷ νηῷ [exaire tous strouthous, kai alla hosa ēn nenosseumena ornithōn genea en tō nēō], he took out the sparrows and the other kinds of birds that were nesting in the temple ^{R3}. The Hebrews, it is true, deny that any birds settled on the temple at Jerusalem, because they were driven off by what they called כולה עורב [II, 594], placed on the very top of the roof. Kimchi on Psal. LXXXIV.: בגג הבית עשו דבר שם כדי שלא ינוח שם עוף והיו קורין אותו כולה עורב, They made something on the roof of the temple so that birds should not rest there, and it was called chole oreb, that is, keeping off ravens. This is frequently mentioned in the Talmud. Thus in the tractate Middoth, ch. 4, fol. 71a, in the Gloss: וכולה עורב מאבד העורבים לפי שהיה מקיף ההיכל למעלה מן המעקה מארבע רוחותיו בחשק של ברזל גובה אמה חד כמו הסיף כדי שלו ישב עליו שום עוף על ההיכל מפני שנחתכים רגליו באותו הסיף, And the chole oreb destroyed ravens, because it surrounded the temple above the parapet on all four sides with an iron band a cubit high, sharp like a sword, so that no bird should settle on the temple, since its feet would be cut off by that sword. And in the tractate On the Sabbath, ch. 9, fol. 90a, on the word לכליא עורב (for so it reads there), the Glossator writes: טבלאת של אמה היו עושין והן חדין כסכין סביבותיה ומסמרין חדין בכלן ומחפין בהן גגו של היכל למנוע את העורבי׳ מלישב, They made plates a cubit in size, sharp all round like a knife and all furnished with sharp nails, with which they covered the roof of the temple to keep off the ravens, so that they would not settle on it. And in the tractate [col. 54] Menachoth, ch. 13, fol. 107a, the Gloss defines כולה העורב as מסמרות חדין תחובין בראש גג ההיכל לכלות העורבי׳ שלא ישבו עליו, sharp nails fixed in the top of the temple roof to prevent the ravens from sitting on it. And another Gloss in the same place: כמין טבלה חדה וקיפה על צידה וחדודה לחתוך כמו סכין, A kind of sharp plate set up on its edge, with an edge like a knife for cutting. And the Aruch [=the ʿArukh of Nathan ben Jehiel of Rome]: עשה צורה להבריח בה העופות מגג ההיכל כדרך שעושין עכשיו שומרי זרעים, They made a μορμολύκειον [mormolykeion], with which to chase birds from the temple roof, as those who guard crops do now. And again: במקדש ראשון ששכינה שרוייה בו לא היו צורכין כלה עורב שלא היו עופות פורחין עליו אבל במקדש שני שלו היתה קדושתו כקדושת ראשון הוצרכו לכלה עורב, Because the divine majesty dwelt in the first Sanctuary, there was no need for a προβασκανίῳ [probaskaniō]. For birds did not fly over it. But it was needed in the second, because the holiness of the second was not like that of the first. Yet something of the kind is described even in Solomon's temple by Eupolemus, when he says ^{d)} that he made δακτυλίους δύο χαλκοῦς ἀλυσιδωτοὺς, καὶ στῆσαι αὐτοὺς [daktylious dyo chalkous halysidōtous, kai stēsai autous] (read δικτύας δύο χαλκᾶς ἀλυσιδωτὰς, καὶ στῆσαι αὐτὰς [diktyas dyo chalkas halysidōtas, kai stēsai autas]) ἐπὶ μηχανημάτων ὑπερεχόντων τῷ ὕψει τὸν ναὸν πήχεις κ΄, καὶ σκιάζειν ἐπάνω παντὸς τοῦ ἱεροῦ, καὶ προσκρεμάσαι ἑκάστῃ δικτύϊ κώδωνας χαλκοῦς ταλαντιαίους τετρακοσίους, καὶ ποιῆσαι ὅλας τὰς δικτύας πρὸς τὸ ψοφεῖν τοὺς κώδωνας, καὶ ἀποσοβεῖν τὰ ὄρνεα, ὅπως μὴ καθίζῃ ἐπὶ τοῦ ἱεροῦ, μηδὲ νοσσεύῃ ἐπὶ τοῖς φατνώμασι τῶν πυλῶν, καὶ στοῶν, καὶ μολύνῃ τοῖς ἀποπατήμασι τὸ ἱερὸν [epi mēchanēmatōn hyperechontōn tō hypsei ton naon pēcheis k', kai skiazein epanō pantos tou hierou, kai proskremasai hekastē diktyi kōdōnas chalkous talantiaious tetrakosious, kai poiēsai holas tas diktyas pros to psophein tous kōdōnas, kai aposobein ta ornea, hopōs mē kathizē epi tou hierou, mēde nosseuē epi tois phatnōmasi tōn pylōn, kai stoōn, kai molynē tois apopatēmasi to hieron], two bronze nets linked with rings, and that he set them on machines which rose twenty cubits above the temple and overshadowed the whole of it, and hung from each net [II, 595] four hundred bells of great weight, and fitted all those nets so that the bells would ring and drive off the birds with their sound, so that they would not settle on the temple, nor nest in the coffered ceilings of the gates or porticoes, nor pollute the temple with their droppings. But in the first book of Kings, where Solomon's temple is accurately described, you will find nothing of the sort; nor in Josephus, although he writes the same of the temple built by Herod, On the Jewish War book 6, ch. 6: Κατὰ κορυφὴν δὲ χρυσέους ὀβελοὺς ἀνεῖχε τεθηγμένους, ὡς μή τινι προσκαθεζομένῳ μολύνοιτο τῶν ὀρνέων [Kata koryphēn de chryseous obelous aneiche tethēgmenous, hōs mē tini proskathezomenō molynoito tōn orneōn], On the top it bristled with very sharp golden spits, so that it should not be polluted by birds settling on it. This agrees well enough with the description of the כלה עורב handed down by the Talmudists. Yet suppose that Solomon's temple too bristled with such spits on the ridge of the roof: this would have kept the birds off the top, but not off the whole roof or the other parts of the temple. If Christ could stand unharmed ἐπὶ τὸ πτερύγιον τοῦ ἱεροῦ [epi to pterygion tou hierou], on the pinnacle of the temple, Matt 4:5, how much more little birds ^{R4}?

notes.text: In that passage rash words and curses are compared with the wandering and circling sparrow and with the דרור. A. Schultens, in his Commentary on this passage, p. 345 ff., shows that the latter may not unreasonably be understood of the swallow, from a similar usage of the Arabs, who are accustomed to denote rash levity by this proverb: طارت عصافيره [ṭārat ʿaṣāfīruhu], his sparrows fly. With this agrees another: طارت خطاطيفه [ṭārat khaṭāṭīfuhu] his swallows fly, customarily used of an empty and rash babbler.
notes.label: R1

notes.text: Merrick, in his notes on the passage, shows from Eustathius and Hesychius that it is not unusual among the Greeks either to put the word βωμου [bōmou], altar, sometimes for temple. Schnurrer [=C. F. Schnurrer, Dissertationes philologico-criticae (1790)], it is true, in his Animadversions on this passage (in the Dissertations Published Together, p. 162), rejects this interpretation on the ground that it cannot be demonstrated by examples that the Hebrews used the word מזבח in the same sense. To me, however, a synecdoche of this kind seems so natural to the poets of every nation that I would recognize it in our Hebrew poet even without the authority of examples.
notes.label: R2

notes.text: Philo, On the Life of Moses, book 3, and 2 Chr 2:8.
notes.label: b)

notes.text: The observation of ANT. DRIESSEN on this passage deserves to be added, from his Specimen of Observations in which Certain Passages of the Old Testament are Explained, Defended and Emended, with a preface by Nicol. Guil. Schroeder, Groningen 1774 (this dissertation is included in the Συλλογη [Syllogē] of Philological-Exegetical Dissertations Published by Various Authors and Defended under the Presidency of A. Schultens, I. I. Schultens and N. G. Schroeder, Leiden and Leeuwarden 1775, vol. 2, p. 1094 ff.): „It has already been observed by others that this passage refers to a custom accepted among ancient peoples, whereby animals dwelling in a sacred building, especially birds nesting in its walls or on the sides of the altars, were regarded as admitted into the protection of the Deity, so that it was sacrilege to harm them or drive them from their abode. Yet it will not be useless or unpleasant to compare an altogether similar passage from the Older Monuments of Arabia [edited by A. Schultens, Leiden 1740], Poem 1, where, just as the Psalmist celebrates the excellence of the holy place and the kindness of the Deity on the ground that even animals find a safe abode there, so Amru Ben Elharith extols the excellence of the Meccan sanctuary in a similar way: ونبكي لبيت ليس يوذي حمامة [wa-nabkī li-baytin laysa yūdhī ḥamāmatun] يظل دها امنا وفيه العصافر [yaẓallu dahā āminan wa-fīhi al-ʿaṣāfir] وفيه وحوش لا تراب انيسة [wa-fīhi wuḥūshun lā turābu anīsatun] انا خرجت منه فليست تغادم [anā kharajat minhu fa-laysat tughādim] And we weep for the sanctuary, whose dove is not harmed, which rejoices secure in its shade, and the sparrows there too; there also wild beasts that are not frightened, tame, even if they go out from it; and they inflict no harm. The reason why I thought it worthwhile to compare this poem with the sacred hymn is that the same animals occur in both, namely sparrows and doves. The celebrated Schultens dates this Arabic fragment to the age of Solomon. Moreover, the particle את in the words את מזבחותיך undoubtedly means at, beside, as often elsewhere.“ Thus Driessen. These remarks, though aptly made, contribute nothing to determining the meaning of the word דרור; for swallows could nest in the temple just as well as wood pigeons.
notes.label: R3

notes.text: In this whole discussion I would think Bochart more successful in refuting the fancies of others than in establishing his own opinion. For at the beginning of this chapter he rightly objected to those who render it swallow, as if it were named from freedom, that this reason is not sufficient, since there are also other birds, some domestic, some wild; yet soon he himself uses the same reason to show that דרור is a species of wild dove. Indeed, our author's whole argument comes to this: the Hebrew דרור, like the Arabic حرّ [ḥurr], means free; but among the Arabs حرّ [ḥurr] is an epithet of the wild dove; therefore the Hebrew דרור, carrying the same notion of freedom, denotes that same animal. How weak this is, anyone understands at once, since among the Arabs حرّ [ḥurr] is not the name of the dove but an epithet of the wild dove, added to the noun ساق [sāq], which signifies the male dove. As for the two passages in which the word דרור occurs, we have seen (note 1 and 3) that the swallow fits the former (Proverb. XXVI, 2.) well enough, while for the other the swallow suits as well as the dove. — Forsskål [=Peter Forsskål, Descriptiones animalium (1775)], in Descript. Animalium in Itinere Orientali observatorum p. 10, mentions among the migratory birds of Alexandria one named Dururi, which comes when the dates have ripened, at the end of October, from Upper Egypt, and, when these have been consumed, leaves after three months. Since Alexandria is not much further south than Jerusalem, Michaelis [=J. D. Michaelis, Supplementa ad lexica hebraica (1784–92)] (in Supplemm. vol. 2, p. 477) suspects that this bird may be the Hebrew דרור; yet he determines nothing certain, since it is doubtful in which letters the name is written in Arabic, دُرُوري [durūrī] or ضُرُوري [ḍurūrī]. Nevertheless, toward the end he adds: “Is it the species of sparrow, of the colour of a nightingale, with a very sweet song, which Shaw [=Thomas Shaw, Travels (1738)] saw around Capsa in palm-bearing places, p. 185, Travels, German trans. 164? See also Buffons Naturgeschichte der Voegel vol. 10, p. 161, German trans. Thus I could have called it Dattelnsperling.” Although Michaelis proposed this with hesitation, Ziegler nevertheless took it as certain, in his translation of Proverbs. — Finally, Paulus [=H. E. G. Paulus, Clavis über die Psalmen (1791)], in Clavis Psalmorr. p. 209, flatly denies that any bird at all is denoted by the word דרור, because it is contrasted with τῷ [tō] צפור, that is, with the whole class of birds. Hence he himself renders the Hebrew word tiny ant, comparing the Arabic ذرّ [dharr]; see Castell [=Edmund Castell, Lexicon heptaglotton (London 1669)] [II, 596] Lexic. Hexapl. p. 77c. But צפור signifies both any birds whatever and specifically the sparrow. An ant, moreover, would hardly fit the passage Proverb. XXVI, 2. (דרור לעוף). Nor can a nest, קן, be attributed to an ant, as is done in Ps 84:4 — I would believe that דרור is an onomatopoeic (ὀνοματοποιητικον [onomatopoiētikon]) name of the turtledove, since all the ancient translators agree on this.
notes.label: R4
